new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Turner 1992, 'undetermined': three levels of accent among overlapping prosodic systems) gives no placement; Adelaar 2004 adds that stress is contrastive with a strong root-penultimate, non-shifting tendency -> refines the undetermined record toward 'lexical/contrastive with penult-of-root default'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Adelaar & Muysken (following Turner 1958 and Karsten 1935) treat Shuar word stress as contrastive (phonemic), while noting a pervasive tendency for stress to fall on the penultimate syllable of the radical (root/stem) and to stay on that syllable when suffixes are added (it 'does not shift'), so that in suffixed forms stress can sit far from the word's right edge. No weight condition, no fixed word-edge rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'pervasive tendency' (i.e. not exceptionless); example (36) wakéra-tin(y)u shows non-shifting root-penult stress; example glosses elsewhere in the sketch carry lexical accent marks (e.g. núwa-ša, nukú-či, úči-ta, atumí) without further comment.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken's sketch is of Shuar (Jívaro) of the Ecuadorian oriente (Morona-Santiago), compiled from Karsten 1935 (possibly influenced by Macas pidgin Shuar, as the authors warn on p.433), Turner 1958, Pellizzaro 1969, Juank 1982, Rouby & Riedmayer 1983, Gnerre 1986 and Beuchat & Rivet 1909-10; spelling not homogenised across sources. Saad 2014 describes present-day Ecuadorian Shuar (fieldwork-based MA thesis); Pellizaro & Náwech 2005 is a Shuar-Spanish encyclopedic dictionary of the Salesian mission tradition (Sucúa/Morona-Santiago).

new_statements.quote: La lengua jívara no tiene regla fija para el acento. En la mayor parte de las palabras, y especialmente en los verbos, se posa sobre la penúltima sílaba. Este acento no cambia cuando, por la conjugación o por alguna partícula pospuesta, la palabra se alarga con una o más sílabas, llegando así el acento muchas veces a caer sobre la cuarta, quinta, o sea sexta sílaba (desde la última). Ejemplos: radical wakéra, querer; wakérahei, yo quiero; wakératiñu, para querer [...] En algunas palabras, el acento también se posa sobre la antepenúltima sílaba, por ej.: aíshmangu, hombre [...] Varios sustantivos y adjetivos también tienen el acento sobre la última sílaba. Por ej.: chimbuí, banco
new_statements.translation: The Jivaro language has no fixed rule for the accent. In most words, and especially in verbs, it rests on the penultimate syllable. This accent does not change when, through conjugation or some postposed particle, the word is lengthened by one or more syllables, so that the accent often comes to fall on the fourth, fifth or even sixth syllable (from the end). Examples: radical wakéra 'to want'; wakérahei 'I want'; wakératiñu 'in order to want' [...] In some words the accent also rests on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. aíshmangu 'man' [...] Several nouns and adjectives also have the accent on the last syllable, e.g. chimbuí 'stool'.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Shuar with an empty rule and no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement held by the project: root-anchored, predominantly stem-penultimate, non-shifting accent with lexical antepenult and final exceptions. Read via the Spanish translation (the open_url item), whose part 7 translates the 1935 language appendix (general remarks, grammar pp. 383-391, vocabulary pp. 392-401); the 1935 English wording itself was not seen. Karsten's data are from the Upano-river Shuar near Macas (fieldwork 1916-19, 1928-29), i.e. Shuar proper. Note that later analyses cited in Peña 2015 (already held by the project) treat Shuar prosody as 'tone-stress' (Turner 1958) or pitc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed (edge-computed) stress rule: the accent is a property of the radical (root/stem), usually on the radical's penultimate syllable (especially in verbs), and it stays put when suffixes and enclitic particles are added, so in inflected words it can sit four to six syllables from the end. A minority of nouns/adjectives carry antepenultimate accent (aíshmangu, píngera, ándara) -- many of these are explained as penult-accented stems plus a fossilized enclitic (-ki, -ru, -chiru, -ma) -- and several nouns/adjectives carry final accent (chimbuí, tunduí, pushí, yakí, ashí). Vowel length is marked separately (macron) and not tied to accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; nothing about tone or pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenult-accented words (aíshmangu 'man', píngera 'good', ándara 'in vain'; uráhinki, turúnduru, apáchiru analysed as stem-penult plus old enclitic; kukuíhkama with verbal -ma); final-accented nouns/adjectives (chimbuí 'stool', tunduí 'drum', pushí 'shirt', yaki 'tall', ashí 'all'). Accent immobile under suffixation (wakéra / wakérahei / wakératiñu / wakéramaka; ayambruamáka / ayambruamákahei / ayambruamákataheitimi).
new_statements.identity_note: Karsten's grammar describes the 'dialecto del Upano' -- the Shuar of the Upano valley around Macas (Morona-Santiago, Ecuador), learned 1916-1919 and revised 1928-1929; this is Shuar proper (shua1257), not Achuar or Aguaruna. The text read is the 2000 Abya-Yala Spanish translation, not the 1935 English original.

tone_statements.translation: According to Gnerre (2010: 47) and Turner (1992: 14) there are also other significant qualities of the Shuar vowels: length, accent, intensity and tone. The present study deals with vowel length; the other features have never been the subject of systematic studies, and for this reason no information is available on their relevance.

readall_conflicts: No direct conflict among opened sources: only Karsten (1935, read in the 2000 Spanish translation) yields a stress statement, and the catalog record for Shuar has an empty rule. Karsten says there is 'no fixed rule', with accent mostly on the penult of the radical and immobile under suffixation, plus lexical antepenult and final cases. This differs in type from the later analyses reported second-hand in Peña 2015 (Turner 1958 'tone-stress', Gnerre 2010 pitch accent for Shuar), which were not openable here; Saad 2014, which would carry a modern statement, is a restricted (request-a-copy) item and could not be read.

tone.quote: Turner (1958: 19-20) consigna también tono fonémico en el S-E "Fonéticamente hay tres niveles tonales y dos deslizamientos o secuencias ligadas de tono, pero todavía no se sabe cuántos de ellos resultarán predecibles" ... Su último informe (19-62.) sostiene que tanto el S-E como el H tienen tres niveles tonales y un ligado ligero de tono alto a tono bajo. Sospecho que el análisis de acento tonal en aguaruna podría ser aplicable a las otras vmiedades del shuar. Pero como fas palabras tomadas de las fuentes mencionadas no marcan el acentO' según nuestra hipótesis, la dejo sin comprobación.
tone.translation: Turner (1958: 19-20) also records phonemic tone in S-E: "Phonetically there are three tone levels and two glides or linked tone sequences, but it is not yet known how many of them will turn out to be predictable" ... His latest report (1962) holds that both S-E and H[uambisa] have three tone levels and a slight glide from high to low tone. I suspect that the tonal-accent analysis of Aguaruna could be applicable to the other Shuar varieties. But since the words taken from the sources mentioned do not mark accent according to our hypothesis, I leave it unverified.
tone.summary: Second-hand: reports Turner's phonemic tone (three phonetic levels, predictability unknown) for Ecuadorian Shuar; author suspects an Aguaruna-type tonal accent (one high syllable per word), untested.
